title: We gave over 600 first-year students at UVM an Oura ring to track their health. Here's what we learned.
subtitle: The Lived Experiences Measured Using Rings Study (LEMURS) uses data on sleep, activity, stress, and anxiety to examine the relationship between these factors and student well-being.
description: LEMURS findings framed as shares of a cohort, for a unit-chart scrollytelling piece.

introduction.value: At the start of Fall 2022, the Lived Experiences Measured Using Rings Study (LEMURS) recruited a cohort of more than 600 first-year students at the University of Vermont to take part in a longitudinal experiment incentivizing healthy behaviors. During the Fall of 2022, we assessed changes in students' sleep, stress, mental health, and other outcomes through a series of weekly surveys. We also monitored heart-rate (HR), sleep, and activity continuously in this cohort using Oura rings.

gad.journal: Events and Behaviors Associated with Symptoms of GAD in First-year College Students (see also JAACAP Open 2024)

steps.description: Let's start by looking at our cohort of ring-wearing students. Of this group, **97% were aged 18 or 19**, drawn from about a fifth of the class.
steps.note: Cohort A. 65% female, 28% male, 6% non-binary — representative of the first-year class.

steps.description: Before the Oura tracking began, participants provided a self-report of existing, diagnosed conditions that were interfering with daily functioning at the time. **We found that roughly one-third of students reported feeling impacted by anxiety or depression.** This group reappears again and again below.
steps.note: Counts derived from the reported 35% of n=582; the paper gives the percentage, not the headcount.

steps.description: Most of these students had experienced one or more traumatic events. Only 28% of the cohort reported none at all on the Life Events Checklist. As we will see in this story, prior trauma was associated with anxiety trajectories and the physiological shape of a night's sleep.
steps.note: Ordered categories — safe to render as a sequential ramp within one hue.

steps.description: Most students got over 7 hours of sleep per night on average. But **about 32% averaged under seven hours a night** across the semester. The cohort average was 7 hours 26 minutes. The typical student's worst night was 5 hours 45.

During weeks of classes, students kept a relatively consistent sleep schedule. But during the Thanksgiving break, when no classes were in session, the median student's sleep period was centred on 5 AM. By definition, half of the students had a later midpoint. Left to their own devices, the cohort's sleep schedule was much later than the typical 9-to-5 day.
steps.note: This is a median, so the 50/50 split is definitional rather than a measured headcount. Say so if you use it.

steps.description: From analyzing 20,167 sleep periods, we found two distinct shapes of sleep. This first one is called the hammock arc: it dips and rises toward waking. The earlier-trough cluster accounted for 36% of periods, and its median time to the lowest heart rate was 33.6% of the sleep period.

The other cluster had a later trough and accounted for 64% of periods. Its median time to the lowest heart rate was 66% of the sleep period. The late-minimum cluster had lower median percentages of deep and REM sleep than the early cluster, while total sleep duration did not differ significantly (p=0.18). Sleep periods in this cluster were associated with students who had impairment from anxiety or depression, a prior diagnosis, or two or more past traumatic life events.

groups.label: Late trough — median lowest-HR time 66% of sleep
Early trough — median lowest-HR time 33.6% of sleep

stat.label: of logged nature time was on campus

steps.description: Most of their logged nature exposure was on campus. A GPS app recorded where students were, and **about two thirds of logged nature exposure fell inside university boundaries**. In the study, on-campus exposure was associated with slightly higher stress, depression and anxiety; this association does not necessarily show that campus exposure caused those outcomes, just that it was different than off-campus nature exposure.

data.each: share of a mean 159.5 logged minutes per student per week

steps.note: UNIT SWITCH: minutes of exposure, not students. n=548 students contributed.

stat.label: self-reported vs. GPS recorded hours per week

steps.description: **Self-reported nature time was associated with lower depression, stress and loneliness. It was also associated with higher positive affect**. Students self-reported an average of 6.06 hours a week in nature; GPS measured an average of 2.66 hours a week. **The felt experience of nature (about 4 hours more than GPS-tracked) was the one that mattered**. Self-reported nature time was also associated with lower depression (b=−0.069), stress (b=−0.048) and loneliness (b=−0.021), and higher positive affect (b=+0.118); all p<0.001

When compared with excercise, therapy, and the control group, **the nature group showed the largest increase in average heart-rate variability (67.9 to 72.5)** across fifteen treatment weeks. The exercise, control and therapy group means changed by +0.9, −0.2 and −0.1. Confidence bands do overlap for most of the semester, so these trends alone do not establish a group difference.
steps.note: NEEDS A SOURCE, AND A PROVENANCE CHECK. This is a four-arm comparison (control / exercise / nature / therapy) with a treatment window, which is not the observational cohort B design the other nature steps describe. Confirm which paper and figure this is before publishing — the same question applies to the depression slope on the step above.

steps.description: At five-minute resolution, aggregate activity peaks aligned in clock time with class schedules: 50-minute Monday/Wednesday/Friday blocks and 75-minute Tuesday/Thursday blocks. Peak timing was similar for men and women, and for students with and without mental-health impairment. The peaks were less apparent over Thanksgiving break.

Remember the one-third of students from the beginning that reported impairment from anxiety or depression? These students showed 2.8% fewer active calories on a typical day during term. The association was not present when the model was run on Thanksgiving break alone. These results do not establish what accounts for the difference, just shows that a difference exists.

groups.label: Impaired — 2.8% fewer active calories in term

steps.note: Same 35% as step 2 — if your sprites keep identity, these dots should not move between those frames. That recurrence is the strongest structural point in the piece.

stat.label: crossed the clinical threshold for anxiety

steps.description: **Half the cohort hit moderate anxiety at least once.** 275 students scored 10 or higher on the GAD-7 in at least one week of the semester. Measured once in September and once in December, three-quarters of the cohort would have looked unchanged. Measured weekly, half of them cross a line.
steps.note: The manuscript labels 275 as both '51% crossed' and '49% never'. 275/541 = 50.8%, so 275 is the crossing group and 266 is the remainder.

steps.description: Interestingly, almost nobody stays on one side of the line. Only 43 students were above the moderate threshold at every single survey, and only 13 were severe throughout. The other 42% moved back and forth. One in five week-to-week transitions crossed up into moderate anxiety; one in five crossed back down.

data.each: 1 dot = 1 student; dot motion is simulated

steps.note: Ordered categories — sequential ramp within one hue. 43/541 = 7.9%; the paper rounds it to 9%.

stat.label: with vs without a prior diagnosis

steps.description: Students who started college with an anxiety diagnosis more often crossed the moderate-anxiety threshold: 153 of 210, compared with 122 of 331 without a prior diagnosis. For severe symptoms, the rates were 41% and 14%. A prior diagnosis was also associated with higher odds of being above threshold every week.

data.each: Each bar is 100% of its diagnosis group; n is shown per row.

steps.note: Each bar shows within-group percentages; equal bar lengths compare rates, not group sizes.

steps.description: Of 3,112 completed weekly survey responses, 1,996 (64%) met the PSS-10 threshold of 14 or higher. These are student-week responses, not unique students or weeks spent stressed; 525 students contributed responses.
steps.note: UNIT SWITCH: completed weekly survey responses (student-weeks), not unique students. 525 students contributed them.

stat.label: among female, nonbinary and transgender students than for male students (as measured by PSS-10 points)

steps.description: In our cohort, 73% of students identified as female, nonbinary, or transgender. And this group ended up showing higher perceived stress levels. Estimated perceived stress scores for these students were **2.5 to 3.4 points higher than for male students**. The range reflects different models, some of which also included sleep measures. The models estimated roughly four to six times the odds of moderate-to-high stress.

data.label: Female, nonbinary and transgender students
data.each: Range across five models, not a confidence interval.
